pr_title: [Merged by Bors] - bevy_reflect: Add statically available type info for reflected types
pr_comments:
This is definitely a good idea to have on hand, since this can be quite useful to have on hand for serialization of trait objects. If this is accessible via `dyn Reflect`, it can be used in place of `typetag` for differentiating the trait object during serialization, though it would require a `TypeRegistry` for deserialization.

This came up when planning out in-memory storage and asset serialization for animation clips where trait objects are required due to the generic parameter on both the trait and the concrete implementation.

I'm wondering if maybe I should also store the relevant `TypeId`s in the type info structs. This might be useful for comparisons where only the `TypeId` is available and its physical type (and subsequently its type name) is not.

> Note: This requires that the reflected type is sized (which I think is generally okay?)

Generally if you see `Self : Sized` on a method in a trait it is "I want to use `dyn Trait` but this method doesn't work like that". In this case the problem is you need to take `&self` or `&mut self` to be object safe so `Self : Sized` avoids the problem by saying "this method can't be called via `dyn Trait`" allowing `dyn Trait` to work (as the non-object safe method isn't available).

This means that `dyn Reflect` can't call `type_info()` as `dyn Reflect : !Sized` which means that method isn't available. To my knowledge the only workaround is to provide a second method that takes `&self` and ignores it as that would be type safe.

I ran into this before digging into `dyn Bundle` but I wasn't able to find any best practices for how to architect this...

> This means that `dyn Reflect` can't call `type_info()` as `dyn Reflect : !Sized` which means that method isn't available. To my knowledge the only workaround is to provide a second method that takes `&self` and ignores it as that would be type safe.

Yeah, unfortunately I don't think it can cover everything while still being statically available. The reason I said it should generally be okay, though, is that I don't see reflection being typically used on unsized types.

I think the biggest issue, which is probably what you're getting at, are sized wrappers around unsized types, like `Box<dyn Foo>`. If we wanted to get that to work, we could probably separate the `type_info()` method from `Reflect`. It was only added to `Reflect` to keep things cleaner (only one trait to worry about), but it could be a standalone trait that's implemented alongside Reflect in the derive macro and impls.

One concern with that is if we wanted to use `TypeInfo` for serialization, we'd have to enforce this new trait as well, which could be annoying for manual implementors. But then again, we really don't expect this to be done manually (the derive macro implements a bunch of other traits as well),

---

@Guvante (or anyone else) Thoughts on this? Should it be a method in a separate trait instead? Maybe something like `Typed` or `Static`?

> One concern with that is if we wanted to use `TypeInfo` for serialization, we'd have to enforce this new trait as well, which could be annoying for manual implementors.

Actually this might not be true. Serialization would probably not need `TypeInfo` since most of the data is already contained within the `ReflectRef`. And deserialization would only get `TypeInfo` from the registry (which doesn't require `Reflect` at all). This means, so long as we can get it to properly register, it should be okay to separate I believe.

However, we'd either need to include the `Typed` (or whatever we call it) bound on `T` in:
https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/blob/83c5e6e72ffc913ccb9ec5cd61e0a57757357082/crates/bevy_reflect/src/type_registry.rs#L222-L233

Alternatively, we can make the `type_info` field an `Option<TypeInfo>`, and set the value in `GetTypeRegistration::get_type_registration()` to `Some(my_type_info)`.

---

Personally I think all reflected types _should_ be required to have their `TypeInfo` available so I prefer the first option.

My point was that you can't call a method that doesn't take `&self` (or `&mut self`) from `dyn Reflect`. Since object safety disallows any methods that break this you can either separate those methods (like you did with `Typed`) or add a generic constraint that prevents the method being called in `dyn Reflect` style situations via `Self : Sized`.

A subtle point I think that got missed while `Box<dyn Reflect> : Sized` you aren't calling a method on it but instead on `&dyn Reflect` via `Deref`. Thus when the trait in utilized in this situation `!Sized` is the situation.

Basically whether you punt the method to `Typed` or use `Self : Sized` the result is the same. You cannot go from `dyn Reflect` to `type_info()`. If you wanted to do so you would need a version that takes `&self` (you don't need to use it).

However I am not following the conversation on whether `dyn Reflect` -> `type_info` is important. If it isn't sorry for focusing on it...

> A subtle point I think that got missed while `Box<dyn Reflect> : Sized` you aren't calling a method on it but instead on `&dyn Reflect` via `Deref`. Thus when the trait in utilized in this situation `!Sized` is the situation.
> 
> Basically whether you punt the method to `Typed` or use `Self : Sized` the result is the same. You cannot go from `dyn Reflect` to `type_info()`. If you wanted to do so you would need a version that takes `&self` (you don't need to use it).

Oh okay I see what you're saying. I think what I want is to be able to do something more like:

```rust
let info = <dyn Reflect>::type_info();
```

Instead of:

```rust
let info = my_dyn_reflect.type_info();
```

So I think I just misunderstood your original point (unless I'm still misunderstanding which is pretty likely haha).

However, I after just reading #3392, I realize that we don't actually implement `Reflect` on `dyn Reflect`, which means this might not even matter all that much until we do (😅). In fact, I'm not even sure `Reflect` would work on unsized types at all.

> However I am not following the conversation on whether `dyn Reflect` -> `type_info` is important. If it isn't sorry for focusing on it...

Yeah, I don't think it is, but this might work for other unsized types at least (again, if that's actually supported or will be supported).

There is no currently supported mechanism for doing `<dyn Reflect>::type_info()` since what trait implementation would be used? Note that while it seems obvious in this syntax the usual syntax is `<T>::type_info()` for some `T : Reflect`. Adding `Self : Sized` ensures that even though `dyn Reflect : Reflect` you won't try and call `<T>::type_info()` for `dyn Reflect` as that will fail to compile (given that `dyn Reflect : !Sized`).

> There is no currently supported mechanism for doing `<dyn Reflect>::type_info()` since what trait implementation would be used?

I'm not sure I follow. Doing `<dyn Reflect>::type_info()` works with the addition of the `Typed` trait.

<details>
<summary>Example Output</summary>

```rust
Value(
  ValueInfo {
    type_name: "dyn bevy_reflect::reflect::Reflect",
    type_id: TypeId {
      t: 14763511120282298915,
    },
  },
)
```
> Granted, this required adding `?Sized` to `ValueInfo::new<T>()`

</details>

Unless you're referring to the original comment regarding the `Self: Sized` bound on `Reflect::type_info()`. I agree that it probably wouldn't work like I originally thought there.

Do you think doing it this way (with the `Typed` trait) helps? Or are there other considerations I might be missing?

A `TypeIdentity(&'static str, TypeId)` struct might be useful in cleaning up a lot of the duplicated code here. For example having a `fn key(&self) -> &TypeIdentity` on `MapInfo` would let you use calls like `map_info.key().name()` or `map_info.key().is::<T>()`.

> I'm not sure I follow. Doing <dyn Reflect>::type_info() works with the addition of the Typed trait.

I think their point is that calling `<dyn Reflect>::type_info()` doesn't return a concrete `TypeInfo` for the underlying implementation, which there is none in this case.

However, I don't see this as an issue, as the main way I see this functionality being used is to lookup static type information about a type in a `TypeRegistry` without a concrete version of the type around: all you need is the corresponding type name or `TypeId`. Attempting to fetch `type_info` from a concrete type is for the most part otherwise pointless since you know the type at compile time.

Another thought: can we make a `fn construct_default(&self) -> Option<Box<dyn Reflect>>` on `TypeInfo`? It would let us make concrete versions of the type to then bootstrap deserialization in cases where we don't know the concrete type and cannot use `FromReflect`.

> Another thought: can we make a `fn construct_default(&self) -> Option<Box<dyn Reflect>>` on `TypeInfo`? It would let us make concrete versions of the type to then bootstrap deserialization in cases where we don't know the concrete type and cannot use `FromReflect`

Yeah I was considering this, but I wasn't sure how we construct the concrete type. It would be easy if they all impled `Default`, then we could just store a function that calls that method. But maybe I'm overthinking it. Is there a better way?

> A `TypeIdentity(&'static str, TypeId)` struct might be useful in cleaning up a lot of the duplicated code here. For example having a `fn key(&self) -> &TypeIdentity` on `MapInfo` would let you use calls like `map_info.key().name()` or `map_info.key().is::<T>()`.

Should this apply to the main type as well? For example, should we remove `map.type_id()` in favor of `map.ty().id()` or something?

If not, and we want to keep those methods, we could also consider doing a trait that provides them (since they're so common). But not sure how I feel about a trait like that possibly cluttering up this crate's exports.

> Should this apply to the main type as well? For example, should we remove `map.type_id()` in favor of `map.ty().id()` or something?
> 
> If not, and we want to keep those methods, we could also consider doing a trait that provides them (since they're so common). But not sure how I feel about a trait like that possibly cluttering up this crate's exports.

That sounds like a good idea to me, since a good number of these APIs are heavily duplicated multiple times over. Not too sure about the `ty()` naming though.

> That sounds like a good idea to me, since a good number of these APIs are heavily duplicated multiple times over.

So should we replace the existing `type_name()` and `type_id()` methods? So they're only accessible through the `TypeIdentity`? Or should we go the trait route?

> Not too sure about the `ty()` naming though.

Me neither haha any suggestions? I was thinking `id()` but `id().id()` might be odd (unless we do `id().type_id()`) 🤔

> So should we replace the existing type_name() and type_id() methods? So they're only accessible through the TypeIdentity? Or should we go the trait route?

A trait seems like it would bloat the interface here. Just having a internal TypeIdentity struct that has a read-only accessor should be enough.

`const TypeInfo::of::<T>` seems to be reliant on the stabilization of rust-lang/rust#77125, which has been blocked for the past few months.
Also wanted to note that this probably supersedes #1922, as it does the same thing but provides a much more information about the type.

Another thought I had: do we want to include any of the following additional information:

* Type data for generics
* Visibility of structs and fields

Generics I think are probably OK to avoid since they get monomorphized out at some point: there is no non-generic version of the type that can be fetched at runtime (for better or for worse). This is not the case for another language (i.e. C#) where there exists this template at runtime that it JITs out a copy of when needed.

Visibility I think isn't too useful here? By using Reflect we're cracking open any opaque type using the `derive`, and opaquely applying value-derived ones. It could be good metadata, but realistically, do we need this info at runtime?
The most recent commits update this PR to the new `bevy_reflect_derive` refactor. They also add a new `ArrayInfo` type to match the addition of the `Array` trait.

I’m wondering if I should just add a `type_info()` method to `Reflect`. Theoretically all `Reflect` types should also implement `Typed`. The reason it's not a supertrait is because `Typed` is not object safe. However, `Reflect::type_info(&self)` shouldn't break object safety. And I imagine it could be really useful for getting type information directly from a `dyn Reflect` (as opposed to just statically).

That being said, you can already get that information from the registry itself vía `get_type_info(...)`. This is generally better to use since it returns a reference (it's not creating a new `TypeInfo` every time). So we could leave it at that, but it might be convenient to have it on `Reflect` itself. 

Any thoughts?
Can we move the `type_info()` method out into a seperate trait and then make that a supertrait?

> Can we move the `type_info()` method out into a seperate trait and then make that a supertrait?

We could do that for `type_info(&self)` yeah. Is there a reason it shouldn't go in `Reflect` itself? (And any suggestions on a name for such a trait?)

Ah, I see what you're doing now. We can't use the `type_info()` method without parameters because it's not object-safe, including if it's a trait method.

Okay, now that I have a better idea of the problem, I'm in favor of just adding this to `Reflect` as well, with cross-links between the docs of each method.

The `Typed` method can be const and doesn't require a reference to an object, but the `Reflect` version will be usable as a trait object, so neither is strictly superior.

> I'm in favor of just adding this to `Reflect` as well, with cross-links between the docs of each method.
> 
> The `Typed` method can be const and doesn't require a reference to an object, but the `Reflect` version will be usable as a trait object, so neither is strictly superior.

I agree. It might feel a little redundant, but I think they each serve a purpose:

* `Typed::type_info()` - _Statically_ create a `TypeInfo` without an instance of a type
* `Reflect::type_info(&self)` - _Dynamically_ create a `TypeInfo` from a `dyn Reflect` without knowing its actual type at compile time.
* `TypeRegistry::get_type_info(&self, TypeId)` - Access a _cached_ `TypeInfo` without re-allocating

So I think it's worth it. I'll add that in and supply the cross-links as you suggested 🙂.

I'm running into one snag with adding `Reflect::type_info(&self)`: dynamic types. 

All `Dynamic***` structs implement `Reflect` in a way that attempts to mimic the actual type. For example, `DynamicStruct::type_name(&self)` doesn't return `"DynamicStruct"`, it returns `"MyUnderlyingStruct"`.

Is it okay, then, that `DynamicStruct::type_info(&self)` returns `TypeInfo::Dynamic` instead of `TypeInfo::Struct`? I think it's okay, but I'm not sure how everyone else feels about this.
My feeling is that this is fine, but not ideal. We can always refactor that bit later if we come up with a good way to make it work.

Okay so I actually decided to call the method `Reflect::get_type_info` to prevent collision with `Typed` itself, which would require users to have to write `<Self as Typed>::type_info()`.

Of course, I'm open to renaming this or even renaming the method in `Typed` instead. Or possibly keeping it as `type_info` if we don't mind the explicit `<Self as Typed>`.

[Previously](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/pull/4042#issuecomment-1061360212), I asked if we should include type data for generics and we came to the conclusion it wasn't a good idea.

With the transition to try and make `TypeInfo` purely static, should this be reconsidered? I'm thinking no, since it makes `Typed` a required bound on all generic type params. But I wanted to throw it out there in case there were different opinions.

Also, on the subject of generics, would it be worth adding a flag for whether a type is generic or not? And accessible via a `TypeInfo::is_generic(&self) -> bool` method? Not sure what immediate value that has, so maybe we can exclude it for now (maybe it could help with serde stuff, though).

Okay, this last commit (a877911bce960f5d1ba2425267be8105d038fa2d) is a big change in the API. Now, `Typed::type_info()` returns `&'static TypeInfo` instead of just `TypeInfo`.

This was done by [suggestion](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/pull/4042#discussion_r876417021) from @cart. Essentially, we reduce a lot of the runtime cost of using `Typed::type_info()` by making things (lazily) static.

What does this mean for those who wish to manually implement `Typed`? In the newly added `utility` module (which is not exported as part of the prelude), I created a `TypeInfoCell` struct. This can be used to automatically manage the `once_cell` logic for either generic or non-generic types. It makes it a lot easier to create a static `TypeInfo` for manual implementors.
Just so we don't forget, @MrGVSV, can you edit the description to say this fixes #4504?

issue_context.title: Static type introspection
issue_context.body:
## What problem does this solve or what need does it fill?

It would be nice if I could get the names and types of fields in a struct, without creating an instance of that struct.

## What solution would you like?

Static methods on `Struct`, `Tuple`, etc. 

## What alternative(s) have you considered?

I could probably make my own macro to get just the info I need. It just feels like this is something that should be in a more general-purpose reflection crate.

## Additional context

My personal use case was an experimental entity-first ORM. I was hoping to use bevy_reflect to help generate migrations, but I needed this feature to make it work that way.

I already scrapped that whole idea in favor of a headless CMS, but I'm sure this would be useful for others.
comments:
Yep, 100%.

Now that I see that, my suggestion of adding a method to `Struct`, `Tuple`, etc, seems a little silly. The new `Typed` trait is a much better idea.

review_comments: Hm, you're probably right that we should just delete it (and the other method too) in favor of just using `id()`.
This TypeId + &'static str type name seems to be a repetitive common combo. Perhaps we should have something for this.
Did not include this module in the prelude. Is this okay? I think it makes sense to exclude it since right now it only contains code that is unlikely to be used directly.
Should these be removed in favor of just ignoring the doc test? I'm of the opinion we should keep them.
I like these; ignoring doc tests is a serious maintainability hazard IMO.
If all this does is wrap `TypeIdentity` do we need this anymore?

I think so because otherwise value types couldn't be accessed from `TypeInfo` (which we get from the type registry).

It also provides some semantics over what the contained type corresponds to— based on the possibilities from `ReflectRef`.

I guess the question is if we want to extend this with more metadata in the future, which is up in the air.

Visibility *could* be included here, but not sure if that is worth the trouble/memory.

Yeah, I don't think there's any metadata we _need_ right now.

But again, I do think this variant is needed so that `registry.get_type_info(type_id)` has something to return.

Opening up your discussion topic here:

> Duplication. There's a bit of overlap with the existing traits/structs since they require an instance of the type while the type info structs do not (for example, Struct::field_at(&self, index: usize) and StructInfo::field_at(&self, index: usize), though only StructInfo is accessible without an instance object). Is this okay, or do we want to handle it in another way?

I don't see a good way to reconcile these approaches. The static approach is "heavy" and involves allocations / hashing / etc. The other is lighter / just uses switches on values. When possible, I think the dynamic approach should be preferred. The one exception I can think of is looking up a field by name on a struct with many fields. The static StructInfo with a hash map will pay a constant "hash the full field string" price, whereas the dynamic field lookup will have to check each string name in each match case until it finds a hit.

That being I suspect for all reasonable struct sizes / field name lengths, the match approach will be better because string comparison can generally "early out" instead of comparing every field. And on top of that it avoids the cost of constructing the StructInfo.

I replaced a few of the duplicates (i.e. things that can be statically known) and easily inferred (i.e. things that can use `TypeInfo` to create default implementations) in 1e7cbd8e0c8f76759c51f87b2821a1b824e5de63.

I figured it should be more approachable now that we use `&'static TypeInfo` and no longer need to construct it every time. Let me know if this should be reverted.
